tagline: A loop through sagebrush country, emigrant crossings and seasonal lakes
intro: The Barrel Springs Back Country Byway loops from Cedarville through northeastern California and Nevada, passing sagebrush hills and flat valley floors beneath the Warner Mountains. Pavement gives way to improved gravel and dirt; the Bureau of Land Management advises allowing at least three hours. BLM presents its Back Country Byways as opportunities to learn the natural and cultural history of these landscapes. West of Mosquito Valley, the road narrows and climbs a fairly steep grade, a distinct change from the flat basin floors.

The corridor crosses an older route: the Applegate-Lassen Trail carried emigrants through Surprise Valley in the 1840s and 1850s. Many emigrant trails followed routes already used by American Indians, and passing livestock depleted forage and frightened away game on which local tribes depended. Settlers later homesteaded on Northern Paiute winter villages at the northern end of the valley. The Enlarged Homestead Act of 1909 doubled claims from 160 to 320 acres; Long and Mosquito valleys later lost more than forty homesteading families.

For a northbound start, follow County Road 1 from Cedarville and take the BLM tour in reverse order. Lake City and Fort Bidwell precede the sagebrush uplands, Mosquito Lake and the old homestead country of Long Valley. The return passes Fortynine Rock and the Alkali Lakes before reaching Cedarville.

moments.title: Fort Bidwell
moments.text: Settlement at the north end of Surprise Valley brought settlers onto Northern Paiute winter village sites. As tensions increased, settlers petitioned for troops, and a military fort was established. The BLM guide records the conversion of its buildings into a regional Indian school and hospital in 1892. The Fort Bidwell Indian Reservation and Cedarville Rancheria remain homes to Northern Paiute people. In town, the guide identifies the community church and Kober’s Drygoods among buildings retaining their century-old appearance. The General Store was built of stone in 1874 to resist fire, a material choice made when this was a remote outpost.

moments.title: Mosquito Lake
moments.text: The byway crosses Mosquito Lake on a levee, with water possible in spring and early summer. That intermittent water provides migrating birds with food and protection: water and mud deter predators. The BLM guide singles out shorebirds with long legs and pointed or curved bills, including willets whose flight reveals a black-and-white pattern. The surrounding uplands hold another source of water: springs fed by melting winter snow supply moisture even in late summer. At the guide’s Basin and Range stop, a short dirt road to the southeast provides a view back toward Mosquito Lake and the mountains beyond.

moments.title: Fortynine Rock
moments.text: Fortynine Rock marked a water stop on the Applegate-Lassen Trail, one of the routes used during the California gold rush of 1849. The first “49” marking is said to have been applied with wagon axle grease, an account recorded in the BLM guide. Emigrants used that material to record initials or the year of their passage on rocks. Here the mark identified Fortynine Camp, the last campsite with good water before the dry floor of Surprise Valley. The guide also describes emigrants crossing Fortynine Lake as they traveled west through this country, with the lake normally dry in late summer and fall.

practical: Mosquito Lake: BLM advises against long trailers and long motor homes on the narrow, fairly steep road west out of Mosquito Valley. Dirt sections of the byway require high ground clearance and possibly four-wheel drive. (checked 2026-10-11)
